To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the semantic composition of adjectives and nouns can be modeled using a matrix factorization technique; (2) this model can be used to predict human judgements of word meaning; (3) a joint model that fuses brain imaging and corpus data outperforms models using either data source alone; and (4) semantic composition of adjective-noun phrases in the brain is a complex process that unfolds over time, and involves multiple areas of the brain.
The neural representation of semantic composition is consistent across different brain regions, and that it is also congruent with the semantic composition of adjectives and nouns in a corpus."

we built a joint model of brain and corpus semantics that is more successful than models that use either data source alone, and we used this model to build an understanding of semantic composition in the brains of people reading adjective-noun phrases that is congruent and complementary with previous work.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the semantic composition of words into phrases, and how that composition is reflected in both text corpora and brain activity.
understanding how the meaning of a phrase can be understood as a combination of the meanings of its constituent words.
the semantic composition of words in corpora, and of phrases in the brain.

this thesis demonstrates that corpus and brain data can be used together, in concert, to learn a better understanding of semantic composition.

this thesis shows that brain imaging and corpus data are complementary sources of information, and that they can be used together with machine learning techniques to learn a more accurate, more interpretable and a more detailed model of semantics and semantic processing in the brain.

the brain and corpora are both valid sources of information about semantics, and that they can be used together, to build better models and gain deeper insight into the processes that govern the meaning and composition of language.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are using machine learning to understand the meaning of words and phrases, and the neural processes that give rise to this meaning.
we have built a model that combines corpus and brain data, and that this model is capable of learning a better representation of semantics than models built on only one type of data.
we can build better models of the brain by combining brain imaging data with data about word usage in a text corpus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
machine learning can help researchers understand the brain, and that the brain can help researchers understand machine learning.
the combination of brain and corpus data can lead to a more complete understanding of semantic composition in the mind and brain.
